analysis.one_liner: Blocks employers from letting algorithms alone hire, fire, discipline, or manage workers, and requires testing, disclosure, human review, and appeal rights.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in any committee before Congress ended in January 2025, so no restrictions on automated management were adopted.
analysis.plain_summary: The No Robot Bosses Act would stop employers from relying entirely on software — often called algorithmic management — to hire, fire, discipline, schedule, or set pay. Any automated decision affecting a worker would require human oversight, testing for bias before and after use, a plain-language explanation to the worker within 7 days, and the right to dispute the output and appeal to a human. Workers could opt out of being managed by an algorithm and be assigned a human manager instead, and a new Technology and Worker Protection Division at the Labor Department would enforce the rules, alongside lawsuits by workers, unions, and state attorneys general.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and job applicants at employers with 11 or more employees — including gig and contract workers — gain the right to a human check on any algorithm-driven hiring, firing, discipline, pay, or scheduling decision, plain-language explanations, appeal rights, and the option to opt out of algorithmic management. Unions and state attorneys general gain new enforcement tools, including the right to sue and to void forced arbitration for these claims.

how_it_helps.text: Employers could not rely exclusively on an algorithm to hire, fire, discipline, schedule, or set pay; a human with relevant experience would have to independently corroborate any automated output.

Workers and applicants would get plain-language notice of how an automated system measures them, full documentation of any decision made with one within 7 days, and the right to dispute the output and appeal the decision to a human.
Workers could opt out of being managed by an automated system and be assigned a human manager instead.

Automated systems would have to be tested for discriminatory impact before deployment and annually, with results made public, and the bill gives workers, unions, state attorneys general, and state privacy regulators the right to sue, with statutory damages of $5,000–$20,000 per violation and attorney's fees.
The bill would void forced arbitration agreements and class-action waivers for claims under the act, and would protect workers from retaliation for complaining.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — from large chains to firms with just over 10 employees — bear the cost of pre-deployment and annual bias testing, public disclosure of results, training staff, documenting decisions for workers, providing human corroboration and appeals, and litigation risk from statutory damages of up to $20,000 per violation (up to $40,000 for willful or repeat violations).
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers that automate hiring and management

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden is real: employers would need pre-deployment bias testing, annual independent audits made public, plain-language documentation for every affected worker within 7 days of a decision, and a trained human to corroborate each automated output — costs that would fall most heavily on small firms just above the 11-employee threshold.

Some provisions are technically demanding in ways that may be hard to satisfy: requiring pre-deployment testing for any 'potential discriminatory impact' and a human corroboration of every output could be difficult for fast-changing machine-learning systems, and an honest supporter would concede it might simply lead employers to drop useful scheduling and productivity tools.

The bill creates a new federal enforcement division with broad inspection and reporting powers and a private right of action with statutory damages of $5,000–$20,000 per violation, which critics would call an invitation to litigation beyond what the harm requires.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefits are substantial: a human check on automated firings, disclosure of how they are being judged, an appeals process, and the right to sue with damages and fees that make lawsuits realistic. The main costs fall on employers — the bill estimates none itself, but testing, disclosure, and human review are real compliance burdens, especially for smaller firms near the 11-employee threshold. An honest supporter would also acknowledge that pre-deployment testing for bias is technically hard and could slow adoption of tools that, used well, might reduce human-manager favoritism. But the bill preserves employers' ability to use these systems — it just requires they be validated, explained, and appealable — and died without any recorded objection on the merits, so the trade was never weighed in Congress.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced, none of which acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2025, so it died without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Suzanne Bonamici introduced the No Robot Bosses Act in the House on March 12, 2024, joined by one cosponsor, Rep. Chris Deluzio.
The same day, the Speaker referred it to three committees — Education and the Workforce, House Administration, and Oversight and Accountability — splitting jurisdiction three ways.
No committee held a hearing, marked up the bill, or reported it to the floor at any point during the remainder of the 118th Congress, which ended January 3, 2025.
Because no action was taken before the Congress ended, the bill expired and would need to be reintroduced to move again.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers using automated systems to hire, fire, discipline, and manage workers keep operating without the testing, disclosure, human-review, and appeal requirements the bill would have imposed.

for.name: Rep. Suzanne Bonamici
for.what_they_did: Introduced the No Robot Bosses Act on March 12, 2024.

for.name: Rep. Chris Deluzio
for.what_they_did: The bill's only cosponsor; original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 12, 2024 and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no report — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Committees on House Administration and Oversight and Accountability
against.what_they_did: Received the bill for consideration of provisions in their jurisdiction and took no action.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Set the House agenda for the 118th Congress and never brought the bill up; the bill had no Republican cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for a recorded vote; both its sponsor and its single cosponsor were Democrats, but no votes were ever taken.

industries.industry: Employers using workforce management and surveillance software (retail, warehousing, gig platforms, large service employers)
industries.note: The bill does not ban algorithmic management, but it requires bias testing, disclosure, human corroboration, and appeal rights, and it exposes employers to statutory damages and lawsuits without forced arbitration. Its interest in keeping automated management cheap and unchallenged runs against the bill.

industries.industry: Vendors of automated hiring, scheduling, and productivity-scoring systems
industries.note: The companies selling these tools would face pre-deployment testing, annual independent audits with public results, and liability when their products drive decisions. The bill requires they operate under human oversight rather than as the final word.

industries.industry: Forced-arbitration defense practice / employers relying on mandatory arbitration
industries.note: The bill voids predispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers for claims under the act, removing a tool employers use to keep workplace disputes out of court. This runs directly against the industry's interest and in favor of workers' day in court.
